title: A View From Somewhere: Human-Centric Face Representations
authors: Jerone T. A. Andrews¹, Przemysław Joniak², Alice Xiang¹
title_audio_script: This paper, A View From Somewhere, published at ICLR 2023 by researchers at Sony AI and the University of Tokyo, rethinks how we represent human faces in datasets. Instead of relying on problematic demographic labels like race or gender, the authors collect over six hundred thousand human judgments of face similarity and learn a continuous embedding space aligned with human perception. The result is a face representation that is interpretable, avoids invasive categorical labels, and captures the continuous nature of human phenotypic diversity.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.necessary: Human-centric face datasets are typically evaluated with categorical demographic labels, but such labels are often missing, legally restricted, biased when inferred, and fail to capture the continuous nature of human phenotypic diversity.
sections.additional: Categorical labels cannot express how similar two same-labeled faces are, and rigid taxonomies erase multi-ethnic individuals and can cause psychological harm through mislabeling.
sections.audio_script: Evaluating the diversity of face datasets almost always relies on categorical demographic labels such as race, gender, or age. But these labels are frequently unavailable, legally restricted to collect, and prone to bias when they are inferred by annotators. Worse, categorical labels flatten the continuous nature of human appearance: skin tone becomes simply light or dark, and two faces with the same label can still look very different. Rigid taxonomies also erase multi-ethnic people and can cause real psychological harm when someone is mislabeled.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.necessary: Face similarity is inherently continuous and observer-dependent, so a representation aligned with human perception can avoid problematic semantic labels while still supporting diversity analysis.
sections.additional: Prior work either cannot embed faces outside the training set or pools all judgments, ignoring the stochasticity within and between individual annotators.
sections.audio_script: The authors argue that face similarity is fundamentally continuous and depends on who is doing the judging. If we could learn a representation directly aligned with human perception, we could sidestep problematic semantic labels entirely while still measuring diversity. Existing psychological-embedding methods fall short: they either cannot embed new faces beyond the training set, or they pool every judgment together, throwing away the differences within and between individual annotators.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.necessary: The authors release AVFS, a dataset of 638,180 human triplet judgments over 4,921 faces annotated with annotator identity and demographics, and introduce a conditional framework that learns a continuous, human-interpretable face embedding space.
sections.additional: Annotator-specific masks let the model study how each person weighs embedding dimensions, revealing that annotators are not interchangeable and that sociocultural background shapes similarity decisions.
sections.audio_script: Their answer is A View From Somewhere, or AVFS. They collect a dataset of six hundred thirty-eight thousand triplet similarity judgments over nearly five thousand faces, and crucially, each judgment records the identity and demographics of the annotator who made it. On top of this data they build a conditional learning framework that produces a continuous, low-dimensional, and human-interpretable embedding space, along with per-annotator masks that reveal how different people weigh different visual dimensions.

sections.heading: Method
sections.necessary: A conditional ResNet18 convnet maps faces to 128-dimensional embeddings and is trained on odd-one-out (3AFC) triplet judgments. Each annotator gets a learnable sigmoid mask that gates the embedding dimensions, so similarity is conditioned on who made the judgment.
sections.additional: Setting all masks to ones recovers the unconditional MDS objective (AVFS-U); conditional variants are AVFS-C and post-hoc AVFS-CPH. A sparsity plus non-negativity penalty makes the surviving dimensions interpretable, yielding 22 active dimensions.
sections.audio_script: At the core is a conditional convolutional network, a ResNet eighteen, that maps each face to a one-hundred-twenty-eight-dimensional embedding. Training uses odd-one-out judgments: given a triplet of faces, an annotator picks the least similar one. Each annotator is given a learnable gating mask, passed through a sigmoid, that scales the importance of each embedding dimension. Similarity between two faces is the dot product of their masked, rectified embeddings, and the model predicts the odd-one-out probability from these similarities. A sparsity and non-negativity penalty keeps the dimensions few and interpretable, leaving about twenty-two active dimensions.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.necessary: AVFS contains 638,180 quality-controlled odd-one-out triplet judgments over 4,921 near-frontal face images, each judgment tagged with the annotator's identifier and self-identified demographic attributes.
sections.additional: Evaluation uses held-out same-stimuli triplets (24,060 judgments), novel-stimuli triplets (80,300 judgments), and comparisons against semantically trained baselines on CelebA and FairFace attributes.
sections.audio_script: The AVFS dataset comprises six hundred thirty-eight thousand quality-controlled triplet judgments over four thousand nine hundred twenty-one near-frontal face images. Every judgment carries the annotator's identifier and self-identified demographic attributes. The authors evaluate on held-out judgments over the same stimuli, on eighty thousand judgments over entirely novel faces, and against attribute-recognition baselines trained on CelebA and FairFace semantic labels.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.necessary: AVFS models predict face similarity more accurately than semantically trained baselines on both same-stimuli and novel-stimuli triplets, while better reflecting human judgment uncertainty (higher Spearman's r on odd-one-out entropy).
sections.additional: Annotator-specific masks generalize to triplets of entirely novel faces, indicating the embedding space is more closely aligned with the human mental representation of faces than label-trained spaces.
sections.audio_script: Across both the same-stimuli and the novel-stimuli evaluations, the AVFS models predict human similarity judgments more accurately than baselines trained on semantic labels, and they better capture the uncertainty in human judgments as measured by Spearman correlation. Importantly, the annotator-specific masks generalize even to triplets made entirely of novel faces, which shows the embedding space is more closely aligned with the human mental representation of faces than spaces learned from categorical labels.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.necessary: Randomly swapping annotator masks across the 80,300 judgments drops AVFS-CPH accuracy from 61.7% to 52.8% ± 0.02%, showing annotators are not interchangeable.
sections.additional: Dimension-elimination shows only 6–13 dimensions recover 95–99% of predictive accuracy, while 15–22 dimensions are needed to explain 95–99% of the similarity-matrix variance, evidencing context-dependent similarity.
sections.audio_script: To test whether annotators really matter, the authors randomly shuffle which annotator mask is attached to each of the eighty thousand judgments and recompute accuracy a hundred times. Accuracy drops from about sixty-two percent down to roughly fifty-three percent, proving annotators are not interchangeable. A dimension-elimination analysis further shows that only six to thirteen dimensions are needed to recover most of the predictive accuracy, while fifteen to twenty-two dimensions are required to explain the full similarity structure, evidencing that similarity is context-dependent.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.necessary: 638,180 human face-similarity judgments over 4,921 faces; 22 interpretable dimensions retained at 61.9% validation accuracy; annotator-swap accuracy drop 61.7% to 52.8%; continuous attributes recovered without any semantic training labels.
sections.additional: 128-dimensional ResNet18 embeddings; 24,060 same-stimuli and 80,300 novel-stimuli evaluation judgments.
sections.audio_script: The headline numbers tell the story. Six hundred thirty-eight thousand human judgments over four thousand nine hundred twenty-one faces. Twenty-two interpretable embedding dimensions retained at nearly sixty-two percent validation accuracy. And when annotator identities are scrambled, accuracy falls from sixty-one point seven to fifty-two point eight percent, all achieved without ever training on a single semantic label.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.necessary: Learning face representations from human similarity judgments, rather than demographic labels, yields a continuous, interpretable, and perception-aligned embedding space that supports diversity analysis without invasive categorical labeling.
sections.additional: Because the conditional framework only needs annotator record-keeping, it generalizes to any human decision-making task, not just faces.
sections.audio_script: The key takeaway is that learning face representations from human similarity judgments, instead of demographic labels, produces a continuous, interpretable, and perception-aligned embedding space that supports diversity analysis without invasive categorical labeling. And because the framework only requires keeping track of which annotator made which judgment, the same conditional approach can extend to almost any task built on human decisions.
